newsitem.title: BOSNIA: Serb power struggle heats up, court convenes.
newsitem.headline: Serb power struggle heats up, court convenes.

text.p: PALE, Bosnia - A power struggle among Bosnian Serb leaders entered a pivotal stage on Tuesday as a constitutional court convened to debate a decision by President Biljana Plavsic to dissolve the parliament and call a general election.
The seven-member court was expected to rule against Plavsic and in favour of government hard-liners loyal to ex-president and indicted war criminal Radovan Karadzic.
But if it does Western governments, which support Plavsic, will try to ignore the ruling and hope to see the election go ahead under outside supervision, perhaps in October.
The court met in the mountain village of Pale, outside Sarajevo, which serves as headquarters for Karadzic and his allies.
The court judges have come under severe pressure from Karadzic loyalists to strike down Plavsic's decision, which has plunged Bosnia's Serb entity into political turmoil, Serb sources said.
Plavsic has already made clear she will ignore the court's decision. She accuses her opponents of rampant corruption and has formed a new political party to stand in the general elections.

The office of the international High Representative to Bosnia, Carlos Westendorp, said on Tuesday the constitutional court only had the right to review whether Plavsic had consulted the prime minister and the parliament speaker before taking her decision.

Simon Haselock, spokesman for Westendorp, said a team of European Union experts viewed Plavsic's move as beyond legal reproach and indicated the High Representative would ignore any court ruling which struck down her decision.
"If it (court decision) doesn't conform to our legal opinion and the Venice (EU legal) commission, it won't be considered to have a legal basis," Haselock said.
The ruling Serb Democratic Party, controlled by Karadzic, kicked Plavsic out of the party last month, accusing her of betraying Serb interests by co-operating with international peace mediators.

Plavsic's supporters in the north-west town of Banja Luka believe she and opposition parties can strip the SDS of its majority by tapping into popular dissatisfaction over allegations of high-level corruption.
She has asked the Organisation for Security and Co-operation in Europe to supervise the elections but Karadzic hard-liners oppose an OSCE role and may boycott the vote.

Political analysts said the conflict showed no sign of resolution and that Serb territory was looking increasingly polarised between the western half in Banja Luka and the eastern half controlled by hard-liners.
Plavsic faces an uphill struggle against Karadzic loyalists who control powerful special police units and official media.
The NATO-led peace force announced last week that it would begin strict supervision of unauthorised special police units, which help guard Karadzic.
